ORDER ON STEPHEN FISCHMANN’S MOTION TO COMPEL EL PASO ELECTRIC
COMPANY’S RESPONSES TO FISCHMANN DISCOVERY REQUESTS 1-1 AND 1-2

            THIS MATTER comes before the Hearing Examiners upon Stephen Fischman’s Motion

to Compel El Paso Electric Company’s Responses to Fischmann Discovery Requests 1-1 and 1-2

(“Motion”) filed September 10, 2026 and El Paso Electric Company’s (“EPE”) Response in

Opposition to Stephen Fishmann’s Motion to Compel (“Response”) filed September 18, 2026.

Being duly informed, the Hearing Examiners FIND and CONCLUDE:

            1.     On July 13, 2026, Mr. Fischmann served his First Set of Discovery Requests on

EPE pursuant to 1.2.2.25 NMAC. 1

            2.     Interrogatory 1-1 requests “[f]or each Valuation of the EPE investment by

[Infrastructure Investments Fund (“IIF”)], performed by or for IIF since closing on July 29, 2020

to the present, provide the following information about discount rates used in or reported from the

process.” 2

            3.     The Notes to Request 1-1 state, “[t]hese requests seek documents in the possession,

custody, or control of the Company, including workpapers held by Sun Jupiter Holdings LLC, [IIF

US Holding 2 LP (“IIF US 2”)], IIF, or [J.P. Morgan Investment Management Inc. (“JPMIM”)].” 3

            4.       Interrogatory 1-2 begins, “[p]roduce the note to the audited financial statements of

IIF, or of the IIF master partnership holding the EPE investment, for each fiscal year since the

2020 closing to the present.” 4

            5.       EPE objected to these discovery interrogatories in their response to the discovery

with both general objections and specific objections to these two interrogatories. 5

            6.       According to the Motion, the parties conferred as is required by 1.2.2.25(J)(3)

NMAC. 6 Mr. Fischmann requested a conference on August 5, 2026, the parties exchanged emails,

and counsel met by videoconference on August 21, 2026. 7 8

            7.       On September 16, 2026, EPE served its First Supplemental Objections and

Responses to Fischmann’s First Set of Discovery Requests. 9 According to the Response, EPE

produced the pre-tax, post-tax, levered, and unlevered discount rates, and the underlying capital

structure and cost of capital inputs, that EPE uses for its own forecasting, for each year from 2020

through 2025. 10

            LEGAL STANDARD GOVERNING SCOPE OF DISCOVERY

            8.       On a motion to compel, the moving party bears the burden of showing that the

discovery it seeks falls within the scope of the Rules and within the responding party’s possession,

custody, or control.

          9.     The Commission’s policy on discovery “favors prompt and complete

disclosure and exchange of information.” 11 The scope of discovery in adjudications before

the Commission is broad. The Commission’s procedural rules state that discovery in

Commission proceedings shall be governed by the New Mexico rules of civil procedure

for district courts, except where inconsistent with Commission rules. 12


          10.    The scope of discovery, as defined in the New Mexico Civil Rules of Procedure,

includes information relevant to the subject matter of the action and information reasonably

calculated to lead to the discovery of admissible evidence:

                 (1)     In general. Parties may obtain discovery of any information, not
                         privileged, which is relevant to the subject matter involved in the
                         pending action. The information sought need not be admissible at
                         the trial if the information sought appears reasonably calculated to
                         lead to the discovery of admissible evidence. A party responding to
                         discovery requests shall provide all non-privileged responsive
                         information then known to the party, subject to the limitations in
                         these rules or as ordered by the court. 13

          11.    Rule 1-026-NMRA, however, also provides for limitations on discovery:

                 (2)     Limitations. The court shall limit use of discovery methods set forth
                         in this rule if it determines that: (a) the discovery sought is
                         unreasonably cumulative or duplicative, or is obtainable from some
                         other source that is more convenient, less burdensome, or less
                         expensive; (b) the party seeking discovery has had ample
                         opportunity by discovery in the action to obtain the information
                         sought; or (c) the burden or expense of the proposed discovery

           12.    The scope of discovery interrogatories is defined in NMRA 1-034(A). Any party

           may serve on any other party a request:

                  (1)     to produce and permit the party making the request, or someone
                          acting on the requestor’s behalf, to inspect, copy, test, or sample any
                          designated documents, electronically stored information, or any
                          tangible things, which constitute or contain matters within the scope
                          of Rule 1-026 NMRA, and which are in the possession, custody, or
                          control of the party on whom the request is served[.] 15

           13.    A request for production only requires a party to produce the documents “in the

possession, custody, or control of the party on whom the request is served.” 16 New Mexico applies

a single test to that further clarify that language: “Whether the party from whom the materials are

sought has the practical ability to obtain those materials.” 17

‘Intermediate Companies,’ which are also subsidiaries of IIF US 2, that are ‘up the ladder’ from

Sun Jupiter.” 18 An organizational chart illustrating the post-closing ownership structure was

           SCOPE OF THE CURRENT DOCKET

           16.      The applicant in this case is El Paso Electric Company. 23 There is no indication in

the materials provided by EPE that any of the upstream holding companies in the Company’s

ownership structure are to be considered as applicants in this case. Nor are any of these upstream

companies intervenors in this docket.

           17.      EPE as the applicant seeks “authority to adjust [EPE]’s retail electric rates in New

Mexico.” 24 Again, no upstream and separate entity is implicated in EPE’s request.

           18.      The information in the Commission’s possession from the former Docket No. 19-

00234-UT, as outlined above, satisfies the Hearing Examiners that the upstream Companies in

question are sufficiently separate from the Applicant, EPE, so as to be considered separate and

distinct from the Applicant. As evidenced in that Docket, these companies own the shares of EPE,

but they are ring-fenced from EPE and are required to “maintain an existence that is separate and

distinct from Sun Jupiter, IIF US 2 and any of their affiliates or subsidiaries.” 25

           19.        Therefore, since these upstream companies are not the Applicant and are not

intervenors or parties to this matter, they are outside the scope of this Docket.

           20.        The materials provided by EPE in response to the Motion satisfy the Hearing

Examiners that EPE has produced the best responsive information to the discovery requests that is

within its possession, custody, and control. 26 The Response contains Exhibit A, the Supplemental

Response circulated to the Parties in redacted form. This exhibit is titled the “Discount Rates and

Inputs Used by EPE for Forecasting Purposes.” 27

           21.        EPE has stated that they do not have access or control of the books and records of

the upstream companies at issue. 28

           22.        Rule 1-034(A) NMRA only requires a party to provide documents in their

possession, custody, or control. This Rule does not require that a party compel production of

documents from a separate corporate entity. The Hearing Examiners find that EPE has satisfied

the requirements of 1-034(A) NMRA, and therefore the Motion to Compel is not well taken.

      IT IS THEREFORE ORDERED:

           A.         The Motion to Compel El Paso Electric Company’s Responses to

Fischmann Discovery Requests 1-1 and 1-2 is DENIED.
